candidates.source_name: Athanasius of Alexandria / Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.28
candidates.source_attribution: Athanasius of Alexandria, Epistulae ad Serapionem de Spiritu Sancto (Letters to Serapion on the Holy Spirit, I-IV), in Select Writings and Letters of Athanasius, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers (NPNF), Series 2, Vol. 4, ed. Archibald Robertson (Oxford / T&T Clark, 1892). PD. Greek text in Migne PG 26 (1857). The Serapion correspondence is Athanasius's principal anti-pneumatomachian work, refuting the Tropici denial of the Holy Spirit's divinity and homoousion with Father + Son.
candidates.draft_body:
Athanasius of Alexandria Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.28 (c. 350 AD)

'And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come' — Athanasius marks the APOCALYPTIC TRISAGION (hagios hagios hagios kyrios ho theos ho pantokratōr) as the ECHO of Isa 6:3's seraphic-trisagion, now-explicitly-Trinitarian in its three-fold-holy. The trisagion is the heavenly-liturgy the earthly-liturgy joins-with (cf. the Sanctus in every Eucharistic-Anaphora). The three-fold-holy is patristically-read as Trinitarian: holy-Father + holy-Son + holy-Spirit, one-Lord-God-Almighty. Athanasius cites the trisagion in Serapion 1.28 against Tropici-pneumatomachian denial of the Spirit's-divinity: the three-fold-holy positively-includes the Spirit in the divine-glory. Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the trisagion as the canonical eucharistic-Trinitarian acclamation.

Athanasius of Alexandria Epistulae ad Serapionem 1.28 (c. 350 AD)

'And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come' — Athanasius marks the APOCALYPTIC TRISAGION (hagios hagios hagios kyrios ho theos ho pantokratōr) as the ECHO of Isa 6:3's seraphic-trisagion, now-explicitly-Trinitarian in its three-fold-holy. The trisagion is the heavenly-liturgy the earthly-liturgy joins-with (cf. the Sanctus in every Eucharistic-Anaphora). The three-fold-holy is patristically-read as Trinitarian: holy-Father + holy-Son + holy-Spirit, one-Lord-God-Almighty. Athanasius cites the trisagion in Serapion 1.28 against Tropici-pneumatomachian denial of the Spirit's-divinity: the three-fold-holy positively-includes the Spirit in the divine-glory. Tewahedo Anaphora preserves the trisagion as the canonical eucharistic-Trinitarian acclamation.
